However, in recent surveys, the correlation has been reversed: four in ten young people between 18 and 24 years old support the right (and two-thirds of them support the ultraderecha), while only two in ten choose left-wing options. This age group now accounts for over three million voters out of a total of 37 million. The most significant aspect of this ideological shift is the rapid and unprecedented growth of the ultraderecha among young people. In the CIS survey of May, the conservative space was divided equally between the Partido Popular (20%) and the ultraderecha of Vox and Alvise (22%) among those under 24. A similar correlation occurred in the 25-34 age group (a contingent that accounts for another five million voters). However, this pattern is maintained, intensified, in the CIS survey of July: the ultraderecha has a 13-point lead over the PP in the 18-24 age group, and more than six points in the next age group (25-34 years). The mutation of the ideological youth in Spain has no precedents. With the country just out of the dictatorship, young people leaned clearly to the left (and their location on the ideological scale reflected this, as they now sit one point to the right). Even in the early 90s, the percentage of young people under 35 who supported the PSOE or more left-wing forces doubled or even tripled the rate of adhesions to the right. The data from last May provides clues about the causes of this change. If the declared voting intention is segregated by sex, the result is very eloquent: among men aged 18-24, Vox outperforms the PP by almost eleven points (and seven in the 25-34 age group). However, among young women, it is the Partido Popular that outperforms the ultras: by 12 points in the 18-24 age group, and seven in the 25-34 age group. In short, the ultraderechization of young men has something of an egoistic rebellion against the advance of gender parity. Nevertheless, Spain is not an exceptional case. Other Western countries are experiencing a sustained rise in extreme right-wing parties with the decisive support of new generations. The recent Polish presidential elections are a good example: the ultra-candidate clearly won among those under 40 (and with a greater advantage among men). And something similar occurred in the German legislative elections, although here the young people radicalized towards the two extremes (AfD, to the right, and Die Linke, to the left). Of course, there are exceptions. In the Canadian legislative elections, the Liberal Party (center-left) won over the Conservative Party (close to Trump) thanks to the vote of those under 35 (and especially women). In contrast, the age group between 35 and 54 leaned towards the conservatives. However, unlike what happens not only on the other side of the Atlantic, in the Spanish case, the low level of education still does not play decisively in favor of the ultraderecha, which is residual among those who barely went to school (46% of them vote for the PSOE). And although Vox is also marginal among the working class, it is starting to have presence among the poorest.

Most agree that the current status quo is Vox polling at or near 27% among 18-24 year-olds, the highest ever, but acknowledge structural constraints and volatility.

Key factors increasing the probability are: recent sharp upward trends in youth support, Vox's highly effective social media strategy, resonance with youth economic and cultural grievances, and broader European patterns of far-right youth surges. These suggest a plausible—though not certain—possibility of a spike above 27%, especially if a salient news event, viral moment, or further weakening of traditional parties align with the timing of the final poll.

No expert considers either Yes or No overwhelmingly likely; most expect a close result hinging on possibly random swings or news cycles just before the last survey.

The odds of them surpassing 27% in direct intention by the end of 2025 are seen as moderate—neither very low nor very high—with a cluster of forecasts placing the probability in the 33%-60% range, and leaning slightly above or below even odds depending on how much weight is given to current momentum versus structural and polling limitations.
